draft.title: Macroeconomic and microeconomic policy
card: Macroeconomic policy
It works on the whole economy by managing aggregate demand, the total spending in the economy. It aims to smooth the business cycle in the short run.
Fiscal and monetary
Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation. Monetary policy uses interest rates, set by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).
Microeconomic policy
It targets how particular markets, industries and firms work. It aims to lift productivity and the economy's capacity to produce, which is aggregate supply, over the long run.
Examples include competition policy, labour market reform and tax reform. They work slowly, because firms and workers take time to change how they operate.
draft.remember: Macro policy steers demand now. Micro policy builds capacity for later.

a.q: Which action is an example of macroeconomic policy?
opts: The RBA lowers the cash rate to boost spending
A law makes it easier for new firms to enter a market
A program trains workers in skills that are in short supply
Rules are changed so that ports run more efficiently
a.why: Changing the cash rate is monetary policy. It acts on total spending across the whole economy in the short run. The other options aim to improve how particular markets work, which is microeconomic policy, even though they may also raise output.
a.clue: Which one changes spending across the whole economy?

b.q: Australia's economy is growing slowly and spending is weak. The government wants a fast boost, and also stronger productivity over many years. Which pairing fits?
opts: Tax cuts now, and competition reform for the long run
Competition reform now, and tax cuts for the long run
Rate cuts for the long run, and tax cuts for the short run
Competition reform for both aims, as it shifts demand and supply
b.why: Tax cuts are fiscal policy. They lift spending quickly, so they suit the short-run aim. Competition reform is microeconomic policy, and it builds productivity slowly over years. The reversed pairing is tempting, but reform is slow to act on demand.
b.clue: Match the quick tool to demand and the slow tool to capacity.

proposal.title: Macroeconomic and microeconomic policy
card: Macroeconomic policy
It works on the whole economy by managing aggregate demand, the total spending in the economy. It aims to smooth the business cycle in the short run.
Fiscal and monetary
Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes, such as a broad tax cut to lift spending. Monetary policy uses interest rates, set by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).
Microeconomic policy
It targets how particular markets, industries and firms work. It aims to lift productivity and the economy's capacity to produce, which is aggregate supply, over the long run.
Examples include competition policy, labour market reform and tax reform that changes how taxes are designed. They work slowly, because firms and workers take time to change how they operate.
proposal.remember: Macro policy steers demand now. Micro policy builds capacity for later.

a.q: Which action is an example of macroeconomic policy?
opts: The RBA cuts the cash rate to steady a downturn
The ACCC takes action to stop firms fixing prices
TAFE funding rises for training in scarce skills
Fair Work rules change to allow more flexible hours
a.why: Cutting the cash rate is monetary policy. It acts on total demand across the whole economy in the short run. The other options change how particular markets work, such as competition or the labour market, which is microeconomic policy, even though they may also raise output.
a.clue: Which one acts on the whole economy rather than one market?

b.q: Australia's economy is growing slowly and spending is weak. The government wants a fast boost, and also stronger productivity over many years. Which pairing fits?
opts: Broad tax cuts now, and competition reform for the long run
Competition reform now, and broad tax cuts for the long run
Rate cuts for the long run, and tax cuts for the short run
Competition reform for both, as it lifts demand and supply
b.why: Broad tax cuts to lift spending are fiscal policy, so they suit the short-run aim of boosting demand. Competition reform is microeconomic policy, and it builds productivity slowly over years. The reversed pairing is tempting, but reform is too slow to give a fast boost to spending.
b.clue: Match the quick tool to demand and the slow tool to capacity.
